definitions.text: To inter. [R.] Southey.
Intoxicating.
Anything that intoxicates, as opium, alcohol, etc.; an intoxicant. Smart.
To make drunk; to intoxicate. The cups That cheer but not inebriate. Cowper.
Fig.: To disorder the senses of; to exhilarate or elate as if by spirituous drink; to deprive of sense and judgment; also, to stupefy. The inebriating effect of popular applause. Macaulay.
To become drunk. [Obs.] Bacon.
Intoxicated; drunk; habitually given to drink; stupefied. Thus spake Peter, as a man inebriate and made drunken with the sweetness of this vision, not knowing what he said. Udall.
One who is drunk or intoxicated; esp., an habitual drunkard; as, an asylum fro inebriates. Some inebriates have their paroxysms of inebriety. E. Darwin.

The condition of being inebriated; intoxication; figuratively, deprivation of sense and judgment by anything that exhilarates, as success. Sir T. Browne. Preserve him from the inebriation of prosperity. Macaulay.
Drunkenness; inebriation. E. Darwin.
Intoxicated, or partially so; intoxicating. [R.] T. Brown.
Not edible; not fit for food. -- In*ed`i*bil"i*ty (#), n.
Not edited; unpublished; as, an inedited manuscript. T. Warton.
An arrow poison, made from an apocynaceous plant (Strophanthus hispidus) of the Gaboon country; -- called also onaye.
The quality or state of being ineffable; ineffableness; unspeakableness.
Incapable of being expresses in words; unspeakable; unutterable; indescribable; as, the ineffable joys of heaven. Contentment with our lot . . . will diffuse ineffable contenBeattie.
The quality or state of being ineffable or unutterable; unspeakableness.
In a manner not to be expressed in words; unspeakably. Milton.
Incapable of being effaced; indelible; ineradicable.
So as not to be effaceable.
Ineffectual; impracticable. [R.] Bp. Hall.
Not effective; ineffectual; futile; inefficient; useless; as, an ineffective appeal. The word of God, without the spirit, [is] a dead and ineffective letter. Jer. Taylor.
In an ineffective manner; without effect; inefficiently; ineffectually.
Quality of being ineffective.

Not producing the proper effect; without effect; inefficient; weak; useless; futile; unavailing; as, an ineffectual attempt; an ineffectual expedient. Pope. The peony root has been much commended, . . . and yet has been by many found ineffectual. Boyle. futile. See Uselesss, Inefficacious.
Ineffectualness. [R.]
Without effect; in vain. Hereford . . . had been besieged for abouineffectually by the Scots. Ludlow.
Want of effect, or of power to produce it; inefficacy. The ineffectualness of some men's devotion. Wake.
Want of effervescence. Kirwan.
Not effervescing, or not susceptible of effervescence; quiescent.
The quality of being ineffervescible.
Not capable or susceptible of effervescence.

Not efficacious; not having power to produce the effect desired; inadequate; incompetent; inefficient; impotent. Boyle. The authority of Parliament must become inefficacious . . . to restrain the growth of disorders. Burke. and inefficacious and habitual impotence to any effect. But the distinction is not always observed, nor can it be; for we can not always know whether means are inefficacious till experiment has proved them ineffectual. Inefficacious is therefore sometimes synonymous with ineffectual.
without efficacy or effect.
Want of effect, or of power to produce the effect; inefficacy.

Want of power to produce the desired or proper effect; inefficiency; ineffectualness; futility; uselessness; fruitlessness; as, the inefficacy of medicines or means. The seeming inefficacy of censures. Bp. Hall. The inefficacy was soon proved, like that of many similar medicines. James Gregory.

The quality of being inefficient; want of power or energy sufficient; want of power or energy sufficient for the desired effect; inefficacy; incapacity; as, he was discharged from his position for inefficiency.
Not efficient; not producing the effect intended or desired; inefficacious; as, inefficient means or measures.
Incapable of, or indisposed to, effective action; habitually slack or remiss; effecting little or nothing; as, inefficient workmen; an inefficient administrator.
In an inefficient manner.
Not elaborate; not wrought with care; unpolished; crude; unfinished.
Not elastic.
Want of elasticity.
The quality of being inelegant; want of elegance or grace; want of refinement, beauty, or polish in language, composition, or manners. The notorious inelegance of her figure. T. Hook.
Anything inelegant; as, inelegance of style in literary composition.

Not elegant; deficient in beauty, polish, refinement, grave, or ornament; wanting in anything which correct taste requires. What order so contrived as not to mix Tastes, not well joined, inelegant. Milton. It renders style often obscure, always embarrassed and inelegant. Blair.
In an inelegant manner.
The state or quality of being ineligible.
Not eligible; not qualified to be chos Burke.
In an ineligible manner.
Not eloquent; not fluent, graceful, or pathetic; not persuasive; as, ineloquent language. Nor are thy lips ungraceful, sire of men, Nor tongue ineloquent. Milton.
Without eloquence.
Not to be overcome by struggling; irresistible; inevitable. Bp. Pearson. The ineluctable conditions of matter. Hamerton.
Incapable of being eluded or evaded; unvoidable. Most pressing reasons and ineludible demonstrations. Glanvill.
Not embryonate.
Incapable of being narrated; indescribable; ineffable. [Obs.] "Inenarrable goodness." Bp. Fisher.
Not apt or fit; unfit; unsuitable; improper; unbecoming. The Aristotelian philosophy is inept for new discoveries. Glanvill.
Silly; useless; nonsensical; absurd; foolish. To view attention as a special act of intelligence, and to distinguish it from consciousness, is utterly inept. Sir W. Hamilton.
The quality of being inept; unfitness; inaptitude; unsuitableness. That ineptitude for society, which is frequently the fault of us scholars. Tatler.
Absurdity; nonsense; foolishness.
Unfitly; unsuitably; awkwardly. None of them are made foolishly or ineptly. Dr. H. More.
Unfitness; ineptitude. The feebleness and miserable ineptness of infancy. Dr. H. More.
Unequable. [R.] Bailey.
Unequal; uneven; various. [Obs.] Chaucer.

The quality of being unequal; difference, or want of equality, in any respect; lack of uniformity; disproportion; unevenness; disparity; diversity; as, an inequality in size, stature, numbers, power, distances, motions, rank, property, etc. There is so great an inequality in the length of our legs and arms as makes it impossible for us to walk on all four. Ray. Notwithstanding which inequality of number, it was resolved in a council of war to fight the Dutch fleet. Ludlow. Sympathy is rarely strong where there is a great inequality of condition. Macaulay.

Unevenness; want of levelness; the alternate rising and falling of a surface; as, the inequalities of the surface of the earth, or of a marble slab, etc. The country is cut into so many hills and inequalities as renders it defensible. Addison.
Variableness; changeableness; inconstancy; lack of smoothness or equability; deviation; unsteadiness, as of the weather, feelings, etc. Inequality of air is ever an enemy to health. Bacon.
Disproportion to any office or purpose; inadequacy; competency; as, the inequality of terrestrial things to the wants of a rational soul. South.
(Alg.)
An expression consisting of two unequal quantities, with the sign of inequality (> or <) between them; as, the inequality 2 < 3, or 4 > 1.
(Astron.)
An irregularity, or a deviation, in the motion of a planet or satellite from its uniform mean motion; the amount of such deviation.
An inequality.
Not equally distant; not equidistant.
Having unequal sides; unsymmetrical; unequal-sided.
(Zoöl.)
Having the two ends unequal, as in the clam, quahaug, and most lamellibranch shells.
Unequally lobed; cut into lobes of different shapes or sizes.
Not equitable; not just. Burke.
To ride over or through. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.
Want of equity; injustice; wrong. "Some form of inequity." H. Spencer.
Having unequal valves, as the shell of an oyster.
Incapable of being The bad seed thus sown was ineradicable. Ld. Lytton.
So as not to be eradicable.
Without energy. [R.]
Having no energy; sluggish. [R.] Boyle.
Same as Inermis.
Unarmed; destitute of prickles or thorns, as a leaf. Gray.
Freedom or exemption from error; infallibility. Eikon Basilike.
Incapable of erring; infallible; unerring. "Inerabble and requisite conditions." Sir T. Browne. "Not an inerrable text." Gladstone.
Exemption from error; inerrability; infallibility. Hammond.
With security from error; infallibly; unerringly.
Exemption from error. The absolute inerrancy odf the Bible. The Century.
Not erratic or wandering; fixed; settled; established.
Without error, mistake, or deviation; unerringly. Glanvill.
Destitute of the power of moving itself, or of active resistance to motion; as, matter is inert.

Indisposed to move or act; very slow to act; sluggish; dull; inactive; indolent; lifeless. The inert and desponding party of the court. Macaulay. It present becomes extravagant, then imbecile, and at length utterly inert. I. Taylor.

Not having or manifesting active properties; not affecting other substances when brought in contact with them; powerless for an expected or desired effect. lifeless; irresolute; stupid; senseless; insensible. of stimulus to effort; but one who is inert has something in his constitution or his habits which operates like a weight holding him back from exertion. Sluggish is still stronger, implying some defect of temperament which directly impedes action. Inert and inactive are negative, sluggish is positive. Even the favored isles . . . Can boast but little virtue; and, inert Through plenty, lose in morals what they gain In manners -- victims of luxurious ease. Cowper. Doomed to lose four months in inactive obscurity. Johnson. Sluggish Idleness, the nurse of sin, Upon a slothful ass he chose to ride. Spenser.
(Physics)

That property of matter by which it tends when at rest to remain so, and when in motion to continue in motion, and in the same straight line or direction, unless acted on by some external force; - - sometimes called vis inertiæ.
Inertness; indisposition to motion, exertion, or action; want of energy; sluggishness. Men . . . have immense irresolution and inertia. Carlyle.
(Med.)
Want of activity; sluggishness; -- said especially of the uterus, when, in labor, its contractions have nearly or wholly ceased. Center of inertia. (Mech.) See under Center.
Want of activity or exertion; inertness; quietude. [R.] These vicissitudes of exertion and inertion of the arterial system constitute the paroxysms of remittent fever. E. Darwin.
Inertness; inertia. [R.] Good.
Without activity; sluggishly. Pope.
Want of activity or exertion; habitual indisposition to action or motion; sluggishness; apathy; insensibility. Glanvill. Laziness and inertness of mind. Burke.
Absence of the power of self-motion; inertia.
Not erudite; unlearned; ignorant.
Not escapable.
To allure; to lay a bait for. [Obs.] To inescate and beguile young women! Burton.
The act of baiting; allurement. [Obs.] Hallywell.
A small escutcheon borne within a shield.
In being; actually existing; -- distinguished from in posse, or in potentia, which denote that a thing is not, but may be.
Having no essence or being. H. Brooke. The womb of inessential Naught. Shelley.
Not essential; unessential.

Incapable of being estimated or computed; especially, too valuable or excellent to be measured or fully appreciated; above all price; as, inestimable rights or privileges. But above all, for thine inestimable love. Bk. of Com. Prayer. Science is too inestimable for expression by a money standard. Lyon Playfair.
In a manner, or to a degree, above estimation; as, things inestimably excellent.
Incapable of being
Want of evidence; obscurity. [Obs.] Barrow.
Not evident; not clear or obvious; obscure.
Impossibility to be avoided or shunned; inevitableness. Shelford.
Not evitable; incapable of being shunned; unavoidable; certain. "The inevitable hour." Gray. It was inevitable; it was necessary; it was planted in the nature of things. Burke.
Irresistible. "Inevitable charms." Dryden.
The state of being unavoidable; certainty to happen. Prideaux.
Without possibility of escape or evasion; unavoidably; certainly. Inevitably thou shalt die. Milton. How inevitably does immoderate laughter end in a sigh! South.
Not exact; not precisely correct or true; inaccurate.
Inexactness; uncertainty; as, geographical inexactitude.
In a manner not exact or precise; inaccurately. R. A. Proctor.
Incorrectness; want of exactness.
The quality of being inexcitable; insusceptibility to excitement.
Not susceptible of excitement; dull; lifeless; torpid.

Not excusable; not admitting excuse or justification; as, inexcusable folly. Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest; for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things. Rom. ii. 1.
The quality of being inexcusable; enormity forgiveness. South.
With a degree of guilt or folly beyond excuse or justification. Inexcusably obstinate and perverse. Jortin.
That can not be execrated enough. [R.]
Incapable of being executed or performed; impracticable; infeasible.
Neglect of execution; nonperformance; as, the inexecution of a treaty. Spence.
Want of exertion; want of effort; defect of action; indolence; laziness.
Incapable of being exhaled. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
Not exhausted; not emptied; not spent; not having lost all strength or resources; unexhausted. Dryden.
Without exhaustion.
The state or quality of being inexhaustible; abundance.
Incapable of being exhausted, emptied, or used up; unfailing; not to be wasted or spent; as, inexhaustible stores of provisions; an inexhaustible stock of elegant words. Dryden.
Inexhaustible. Thomson.
To exist within; to dwell within. [Obs.] Substances inexisting within the divine mind. A. Tucker.
Inexistent; not existing. [Obs.] Gudworth.
Want of being or existence.
Not having being; not existing.
Inherent; innate; indwelling. Boyle.
The quality of being inexorable, or unyielding to entreaty. Paley.

Not to be persuaded or moved by entreaty or prayer; firm; determined; unyielding; unchangeable; inflexible; relentless; as, an inexorable prince or tyrant; an inexorable judge. "Inexorable equality of laws." Gibbon. "Death's inexorable doom." Dryden. You are more inhuman, more inexorable, O, ten times more than tigers of Hyrcania. Shak.
The quality or state of being inexorable. Chillingworth.
In an inexorable manner; inflexibly. "Inexorably firm." Thomson.
Incapable of expansion, enlargement, or extension. Tyndall.
Not to be expected or anticipated. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
Not expectant. C. Bronté.
Absence of expectation. Feltham.
Unexpected. [Obs.]
Unexpectedly. [Obs.]
Unexpectedness. [Obs.]

The quality or state of being inexpedient; want of fitness; unsuitableness to the end or object; impropriety; as, the inexpedience of some measures. It is not the rigor but the inexpediency of laws and acts of authority which makes them tyrannical. Paley.

Not expedient; not tending to promote a purpose; not tending to the end desired; inadvisable; unfit; improper; unsuitable to time and place; as, what is expedient at one time may be inexpedient at another. If it was not unlawful, yet it was highly inexpedient to use those ceremonies. Bp. Burnet. inadvisable; disadvantageous.
Not
Not expensive; cheap.

Absence or want of experience; lack of personal and experimental knowledge; as, the inexperience of youth. Failings which are incident to youth and inexperience. Dryden. Prejudice and self-sufficiency naturally proceed from inexperience of the world, and ignorance of mankind. Addison.
Not having experience unskilled. "Inexperienced youth." Cowper.
Destitute of experience or of much experience. [Obs.] Milton.
Not expert; not skilled; destitute of knowledge or dexterity derived from practice. Akenside.
Want of expertness or skill.
Admitting of no expiation, atonement, or satisfaction; as, an inexpiable crime or offense. Pomfret.
Incapable of being mollified or appeased; relentless; implacable. [Archaic] "Inexpiable hate." Milton. They are at inexpiable war with all establishments. Burke.
Quality of being inexpiable.
In an inexpiable manner of degree; to a degree that admits of no atonement.
Not appeased or placated. [Obs.] To rest inexpiate were much too rude a part. Chapman.
Incapable of being explained; inexplicable.
Insatiably. [Obs.] Sandys.
The quality or state of being inexplicable. H. Spencer.

Not explicable; not explainable; incapable of being explained, interpreted, or accounted for; as, an inexplicable mystery. "An inexplicable scratching." Cowper. Their reason is disturbed; their views become vast and perplexed, to others inexplicable, to themselves uncertain. Burke.
A state of being inexplicable; inexplicability.
In an inexplicable manner.
Not explicit; not clearly stated; indefinite; vague.
Incapable of being explored, searched out, or discovered. Sir G. Buck.
Not explosive.
A state of not being exposed.

Not capable of expression or utterance in language; ineffable; unspeakable; indescribable; unutterable; as, inexpressible grief or pleasure. "Inexpressible grandeur." Blair. In orbs Of circuit inexpressible they stood. Milton.
Breeches; trousers. [Colloq. or Slang] Ld. Lytton.
In an inexpressible manner or degree; unspeakably; unutterably. Spectator.
Inexpressible. [R.]
Without expression or meaning; not expressive; dull; unintelligent; as, an inexpressive countenance.
The state or quality of being inexpressive.
Incapable of being subdued by force; impregnable; unconquerable. Burke. A fortress, inexpugnable by the arts of war. Milman.
So as to be inexpugnable; in an inexpugnable manner. Dr. H. More.
Not capable of being passed over; insuperable; insurmountable.
Not extended.
Not capable of being extended; not elastic; as, inextensible fibers.
Want of extension; unextended state.
Incapable of extermination. Rush.
Not quenched; not extinct.
Inextinguishable. [Obs.] Sir T. More.
Not capable of being extinguished; extinguishable; unquenchable; as, inextinguishable flame, light, thirst, desire, feuds. "Inextinguishable rage." Milton.
So as not to be extinguished; in an inextinguishable manner.
Not capable of being extirpated or rooted out; ineradicable.

Incapable of being extricated, untied, or disentangled; hopelessly intricate, confused, or obscure; as, an inextricable knot or difficulty; inextricable confusion. Lost in the wild, inextricable maze. Blackmore.
Inevitable. [R.] "Fate inextricable." Milton.
The state of being inextricable.
In an inextricable manner.
To ingraft, as a tree or plant, by the insertion of a bud or eye; to inoculate. The arts of grafting and ineying. J. Philips.
